subtype: Approach: pausing and recognising pressure tactics [Thinking]
passage: The phone rang while Balram was eating, an unknown number. “This is the bank's customer care. Your father's account will be locked within ten minutes unless you read out the code we just sent.” A message had indeed landed with six digits. Balram's fingers went cold; his father had gone to the fields with the passbook. He almost read it out. Then he whispered to himself, “Why ten minutes? Why would a bank rush me? The rush is what they want.” He said, “I'll call the branch,” and the line went dead. His mother Urmila put down the roti. “Who was that?” “Someone who wanted the code, Ma. Nobody real ever asks for it.” They wrote the number on a scrap to show his father that evening.

qa.q: How many minutes did the caller say the account had?
qa.a: Ten minutes.

qa.q: What was Balram feeling when the message with the code arrived?
qa.a: Fear: his fingers went cold and he almost read the code out.

qa.q: What else could Balram do next, and why?
qa.a: Tell his father and ring the bank on the number in the passbook, since only an official channel can confirm whether the account is safe.

qa.q: How does the call look to Urmila?
qa.a: Urmila hears only one side and sees her son shaken by an unknown caller asking for a code, so she may be relieved that he stopped.

grounding: A teen gets a call with a ten-minute threat about his father's account and treats the urgency itself as the warning sign.

subtype: Approach: hanging up and verifying through an official channel [Action]
passage: “Ankita, you asked what I did when the bank called, so here it is. I'm Preeti, by the way. A man said my account would be frozen unless I confirmed a code. My hands were sweating, and I kept thinking, what if it's real? But I said, ‘I'll call you back,’ and he gave me a number, and something felt off. So I hung up and did not call it. I found my mother and said, ‘Can you phone the bank on the number printed on your card?’ She did. It took a while on hold. Then the woman at the bank said there was no block on any account, and that they never ask for codes on calls. My mother put her hand on my shoulder. I still felt a bit shaky.”

qa.q: Whose number did Preeti's mother phone the bank on?
qa.a: The number printed on her card.

qa.q: How did Preeti feel while the call was happening?
qa.a: Anxious: Preeti's hands were sweating and Preeti kept thinking it might be real, yet chose to check instead of trusting the number.

qa.q: What else could Preeti do after learning it was fake, and why?
qa.a: Tell other family members and report the number, since scammers try the same script on many people.

qa.q: How does the situation look to Preeti's mother?
qa.a: Preeti's mother gets a straight answer from the bank on the official number and sees that Preeti was careful, which is reassuring.

grounding: A student ends the call, does not use the number given and has the mother phone the bank on the card number, learning no block exists.

subtype: Approach: following a rule set in advance [Thinking]
passage: “Simran, I'll tell you about the night I was fifteen and a stranger rang. I'm Karthik, your Mama. Years ago, my father sat us all down and made one rule: OTPs, PINs and passwords stay secret from everyone. Not with the bank, not with the police, not with me. We didn't argue about it. That night the caller was polite. He knew my name and my father's, and said the account was in danger. I said, ‘Sir, family rule. I can't give any code.’ His voice hardened. He said I would be sorry. I put the phone down and my heart was pounding, but I didn't have to decide anything, because it was already decided.”

qa.q: What was the family rule?
qa.a: OTPs, PINs and passwords stay secret from everyone.

qa.q: How did Karthik feel when the caller's voice hardened?
qa.a: Shaky, with a pounding heart, but steady: he did not have to argue because the answer was already decided.

qa.q: Which choice in the story kept Karthik safe, and why?
qa.a: Following the family rule without debating it, because a convincing voice cannot talk someone out of an answer already agreed.

qa.q: How might Karthik's father have felt when he heard about the call?
qa.a: He was probably relieved and proud that the rule had worked, and glad it had been agreed at the family table beforehand.

grounding: An elder recalls a family rule set in advance that lets a teen refuse a convincing caller without debating.

subtype: Approach: reporting to parents and the official cybercrime channel [Action]
passage: “Hemant, honestly, I nearly did it. I'm Sachin. I got a message saying my card had a problem and I should confirm my details through a link. The page looked real, and I had half of my card number typed before something stopped me. It was the little voice that said, why would a bank text me a link? I closed it. Then I didn't just delete it. I took a screenshot and showed my parents at dinner. Nobody shouted. Dad found the official cybercrime website and we reported it together, and Mum phoned the bank on the number on the back of the card, so they could watch for anything odd. It felt better than pretending nothing had happened.”

qa.q: What did Sachin take a screenshot of?
qa.a: The message asking for card details.

qa.q: What did Sachin feel at the moment before closing the page?
qa.a: Tempted and rushed, then uneasy enough to stop when the little voice asked why a bank would send a link.

qa.q: What else could Sachin do, and why?
qa.a: Warn friends about the message, since scammers often send the same one to many people.

qa.q: How does this look to Sachin's parents?
qa.a: They are relieved that Sachin told them instead of quietly deleting the message, and glad to report it and tell the bank so it can watch for odd activity.

grounding: After a suspicious link asking for card details, a teen tells parents, screenshots the message and they report it to the cybercrime portal and bank.

subtype: Approach: trusting a caller who knows some personal details [Pitfall]
passage: Wednesday night. I feel sick. A man phoned this evening and said he was from the scholarship office. He knew my school's name. He knew Abbu's name. So I thought he must be real, and I stopped being careful. He asked my class, my date of birth, Abbu's phone number, which bank we use. I told him everything because he was so kind and said he was just helping. Then he said a code would arrive and I should read it out. My hand was already on the phone screen when my brother Kunal came in and said, “Who is that? Hang up!” I did. I don't know what I gave away. Tomorrow I have to tell Abbu. — Farida

qa.q: What details did the caller already know?
qa.a: The school's name and Abbu's name.

qa.q: How does Farida feel at the end of the entry?
qa.a: Sick with worry and ashamed: Farida does not know what was given away.

qa.q: What could Farida do next, and why?
qa.a: Tell Abbu and the family straight away so the bank can be warned, since the details already given could be misused.

qa.q: How does the call look to Kunal, who walks in?
qa.a: Kunal hears a stranger asking a sibling for a code, recognises the danger at once and tells them to hang up.

grounding: A student trusts a caller who knows the school name and the father's name, and keeps sharing information to be helpful.

subtype: Approach: greed-driven engagement with a prize offer [Pitfall]
passage: Counsellor's note, Thursday. Swati (Class 9) came to my room looking pale. She told me a message had promised a free phone if she paid a small delivery fee. She had imagined the phone in her hand all evening. She paid two hundred rupees using a wallet, and then a second message asked for more. When she ignored it, the messages stopped and the phone never came. “I feel so stupid,” she said. I told her scammers depend on excitement, not on people being foolish, and that it was not her fault. We rang her parents that afternoon, and they reported it to the bank. Swati asked me to help her write a short rule: free things never need payment first. — Jasleen

qa.q: How did Swati pay the fee?
qa.a: Using a wallet.

qa.q: What was Swati feeling after the messages stopped?
qa.a: Embarrassed and upset: she said she felt stupid and blamed herself.

qa.q: What could Swati do next time, and why?
qa.a: Treat any prize that asks for money first as a warning, and check with an adult before paying, since real prizes do not need a payment up front.

qa.q: How does the situation look to the counsellor?
qa.a: Jasleen sees a student tricked through excitement instead of foolishness, and wants her to feel supported and not blamed.

grounding: A teen imagines winning a free phone and pays a small fee, discovering that free prizes needing payment are a standard trick.

subtype: Approach: hiding a mistake out of embarrassment [Pitfall]
passage: On Monday evening in London, Amara clicked a link in a message that said the school account had a problem. The page looked right, and Amara typed the password before thinking. Then the stomach dropped. A face went hot. Surely nobody would ever need to know. For two days Amara said nothing, and lay awake, hoping that it would just go away. On Wednesday Selin, in the same class, showed Amara a message that had come from Amara's account: a strange note asking for money. “Was this you?” Selin asked. Amara's throat closed. Then it all came out. They went together to Amara's mother, and the password was changed that night, but the account had been used for two days.

qa.q: How many days did Amara stay silent?
qa.a: Two days.

qa.q: What was Amara feeling that kept the silence going for two days?
qa.a: Shame: Amara felt the face go hot and hoped nobody would ever need to know.

qa.q: What should Amara have done straight away, and why?
qa.a: Tell a trusted adult and change the password at once, since speed limits what a scammer can do with the account.

qa.q: How does the situation look to Selin?
qa.a: Selin received a strange money request from Amara's account and was suspicious and worried, and by asking directly helped bring the problem into the open.

grounding: After clicking a fake link and entering a password, a teen says nothing for two days out of shame, giving scammers time.

subtype: Approach: containing the damage after a slip [Revision]
passage: I typed my email password into the page, pressed enter, and knew straight away. The page had loaded slowly and the address at the top looked odd. My stomach dropped, and for a few seconds I just stared. Then I stopped panicking and started doing things. First I changed the password on the real site. Then I signed out of every other device. I switched on two-step verification. Finally I went to find Papa, Jatin to everyone else, and said, “I made a mistake, and I think I've fixed most of it, but the bank should know.” He rang the bank that evening while I sat beside him. I still felt silly, but I'd rather say it early than late. — Deepak

qa.q: What did Deepak do first after realising the page was fake?
qa.a: Changed the password on the real site.

qa.q: What did Deepak feel when realising the mistake?
qa.a: Panic and a sinking stomach, but Deepak moved on to doing things instead of freezing.

qa.q: What else could Deepak do in the following days, and why?
qa.a: Watch for odd messages or activity on the account, since a slip may show up only later.

qa.q: How does the situation look to Jatin?
qa.a: Jatin, told the same evening, sees that Deepak acted quickly and responsibly, and can warn the bank while it still matters.

grounding: After entering a login on a fake page, a student changes the password, logs out other devices, turns on two-step verification and tells a parent.

subtype: Approach: mental rehearsal of scam scripts [Thinking]
passage: Uncle Jagdish pinned a printed article to our fridge: fake officers, fake job offers, fake parcels. I read it twice and then did something a bit silly. In front of the bathroom mirror, out loud, I practised. “I will call the police station myself.” “I don't discuss money on the phone.” “Thank you, no.” I said them until they sounded boring, which was the point. A week later my phone rang. A grave voice said there was a parcel in my name with something illegal inside. My hands shook. But the lines were already in my mouth, and I said, “I'll call the station myself,” and ended the call. Then I told Mama and sat down. — Mehr

qa.q: Where did the narrator practise the lines?
qa.a: In front of the bathroom mirror.

qa.q: How did Mehr feel when the real call came?
qa.a: Nervous: Mehr's hands shook, but the practised words came out anyway.

qa.q: What else could Mehr add to the plan, and why?
qa.a: A rule to hang up and tell an adult whatever the caller says, since a calm exit works even when the story sounds frightening.

qa.q: How might Jagdish feel on hearing what happened?
qa.a: Jagdish, who pinned the article, may feel relieved and proud that the reading turned into a calm refusal.

grounding: After reading examples of frauds, a teen rehearses aloud what to say to a fake officer, so a calm refusal is ready.

subtype: Approach: teaching the plan to grandparents [Action]
passage: At the community centre's senior club, Baljeet unrolled a sheet of chart paper and taped it to the board. Three lines in big Hindi letters. Line one: OTP किसी को नहीं बताना, never share the OTP. Line two: फ़ोन काटो, परिवार को फ़ोन करो, put the phone down and ring the family. Line three: इनाम के लिए पैसे नहीं देना, no money for prizes. Baljeet read each line aloud and asked the group to repeat it. Baljeet's grandfather Kunal squinted, then nodded. “Short enough that I'll remember.” His wife, Baljeet's grandmother, asked for a copy. That evening Baljeet taped a smaller sheet next to the landline at home, at the height of Dada's eyes.

qa.q: What are the three rules on the chart?
qa.a: Never share the OTP, put the phone down and ring the family, and no money for prizes.

qa.q: What might Baljeet be feeling as the group repeats the lines?
qa.a: Proud and a little anxious: Baljeet hopes the grandparents will really remember them when the phone rings.

qa.q: What else could Baljeet do to help them remember, and why?
qa.a: Practise a pretend call with them at home, since saying the lines aloud once makes them easier to use under pressure.

qa.q: How does the list look to Baljeet's grandfather?
qa.a: Kunal finds it short and clear, in a language he reads easily, so it is something he can hold onto when a caller sounds convincing.

grounding: A teen writes a short Hindi list for grandparents and posts it near the landline.
